bib.title: LLM in a flash: Efficient Large Language Model Inference with Limited Memory

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LLM in a flash: Efficient Large Language Model Inference with Limited Memory", Keivan Alizadeh, Iman Mirzadeh, Dmitry Belenko, S. Karen Khatamifard, Minsik Cho, Carlo C Del Mundo, Mohammad Rastegari, Mehrdad Farajtabar (Apple). The PDF is arXiv:2312.11514v3 [cs.CL], 30 Jul 2024. The text names no venue, so treat it as a preprint (the cs.CL tag is the only label). First posted Dec 2023, per the arXiv id.

COVERAGE: 87,706 of 87,706 chars read, including appendices A-G. Only the remaining qualitative-sample tables (Tables 7-9, generated text) were skimmed after Table 7. No extraction faults except a stray "«cite nucleus»" in the text. Figures were not viewed. Figure values come from the extracted axis labels only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Headline: models up to 2x the available DRAM run, with up to 4x (CPU) and 20x (GPU) speedup over naive loading.
  number: 4x CPU, 20x GPU. The intro says 4x, 7x and 20x for CPU, Metal and NVIDIA GPU.
  setup: about half of the model size available in DRAM, batch 1 (one sequence at a time), 128-token prompt, 256 generated tokens, C4 validation subset. Naive baseline reloads on demand.
  quote: "run models 2x larger than the device's DRAM capacity and speed up inference up to 4x, 7x, and 20x compared to naive implementation in CPU, Metal and NVIDIA GPU backends, respectively"
  where: Sec 1, p2
- The Discussion widens the range for OPT.
  number: 4-5x on CPU, 20-25x on GPU.
  quote: "on OPT model, we achieve an acceleration in inference speed of 4-5x compared to traditional loading methods in CPU, and 20-25x in GPU"
  where: Sec 7
- Ablation of I/O latency (Table 2). OPT 6.7B, 16-bit, M1 Max, half of memory available.
  Rows (Predictor / Windowing / Bundling, DRAM GB, Flash->DRAM GB, throughput, I/O latency):
  - Naive: 0 GB, 13.4 GB, 6.10 GB/s, 2196 ms.
  - Predictor (hybrid) only: 6.7 GB, 6.7 GB, 6.10 GB/s, 1090 ms.
  - + Windowing: 4.8 GB, 0.9 GB, 1.25 GB/s, 738 ms.
  - + Windowing, DRAM row shows 6.5 GB, 0.2 GB, 1.25 GB/s, 164 ms (a further windowing configuration in the table).
  - + Bundling: 6.5 GB, 0.2 GB, 2.25 GB/s, 87 ms.
  quote (final row): "✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 6.5 0.2 GB 2.25 GB/s 87 ms"
  quote (naive row): "✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ 0 13.4 GB 6.10 GB/s 2196 ms"
  quote (bundling): "bundling technique can alleviate this by doubling the data transfer chunk size and hence the throughput which leads to reducing the overall latency to half."
  where: Table 2, Sec 4.2
  note: the extraction merges the checkmark columns. The 4th row is predictor + windowing + one more optimisation, and the 5th adds bundling. Check Table 2 in the PDF for the exact tick pattern of rows 3-4.
- End-to-end per-token latency in ms (Table 3), I/O + Mem + Compute = Total.
  - OPT 6.7B CPU: Naive 3182, All 669 (I/O 105, Mem 58, Compute 506), about 4.8x.
  - OPT 6.7B Metal M1: Naive 2389, All 565.
  - OPT 6.7B Metal M2: Naive 2270, All 305.
  - OPT 6.7B GPU (RTX 4090, bfloat16): Naive 2218, All 84 (I/O 30, Mem 34, Compute 20), about 26x. Speculative GPU: 60 (I/O 38.5, Mem 9.5, Compute 12).
  - Falcon 7B CPU: Naive 3095, Hybrid 1947, All 706.
  - Persimmon 8B CPU: Naive 3806, Hybrid 2495, All 1041.
  - Phi-2 2.7B CPU: Naive 1287, Hybrid 711, All 546.
  - Llama 2 7B CPU: Naive 3095, Hybrid 1903, All 994.
  quote: "OPT 6.7B All GPU 30 34 20 84"
  quote: "OPT 6.7B Naive GPU 2196 0 22 2218"
  where: Table 3, Sec 4.2. Table 5 gives std devs, e.g. OPT GPU All "84.64 ( ±6.16)".
  setup: about 50% of model size in DRAM for OPT, Falcon, Persimmon and Llama 2. Phi-2 gets 65% because it is small and has less sparsity.
- The baseline is optimistic for the naive method. Per-method I/O latency is a "best theoretical" number, and the naive method is credited with loading only half the model.
  quote: "We used best theoretical possible numbers for IO latency for each of the methods to make a fair comparison, the real number might be higher."
  where: Sec 4.1
- Row-column bundling doubles the read chunk, from d_model*num_bytes to 2*d_model*num_bytes.
  number: 32 KiB per read for 32-bit OPT 6.7B, 35.5 KiB for Falcon 7B 32-bit (as printed).
  quote: "the data chunk size per read is 2dmodel × 4 bytes = 32KiB"
  where: Sec 3.2, App C.1
- Flash hardware facts.
  number: over 6 GiB/s for a 1 GiB linear read, versus 1.25 GiB/s sparse reads.
  setup: MacBook M1 Max, 1 TB flash, uncached file. Reads use 32 threads. 32 KiB or larger random reads across multiple threads give enough throughput. Figure 2a sketches DRAM ~100 GB/s vs flash ~1 GB/s, and ~100 GB vs ~10 GB capacity.
  quote: "speeds exceeding 6 GiB/s for a 1GiB linear read of an uncached file"
  quote: "throughputs appropriate for sparse LLM inference are achievable on modern hardware using 32KiB or larger random reads across multiple threads"
  quote: "1.25 GiB/s sparse vs 6.1 GiB/s dense"
  where: Sec 2.2, 4.2
- It can pay to read more than needed.
  quote: "in some scenarios, it will be worthwhile to read more than needed (but in larger chunks) and then discard"
  where: Sec 2.2
- Activation sparsity the method relies on.
  number: OPT 6.7B 97%, Falcon 7B (relufied) 95%, Llama 2 (FATReLU, finetuned) 90%.
  quote: "The OPT 6.7B model, for instance, exhibits a notable 97% sparsity within its FFN layer."
  where: Sec 3.1
- Windowing. Keep in DRAM the neurons active for the last k tokens and load only the increment s_agg(k+1) - s_agg(k). Figure 4 uses k=5.
  number: OPT 6.7B with k=4. The predictor's active neurons alone would take about 10% of DRAM, windowing drops new loads to 2.4% per token, and the window of the past 5 tokens raises FFN DRAM to 24%. Total DRAM is 52.1% of the model: predictor 1.25%, embeddings 3%, attention 32.3%, FFN 15.5%.
  quote: "Using active neurons of predictor would require about 10% of the DRAM memory capacity on average; however, with our method, it drops to 2.4%."
  where: App C.1
- Predictors are low-rank and use the current layer's attention output, unlike Dejavu, which uses the previous layer.
  setup: OPT 6.7B has rank 128 for the first 28 layers and 1024 for the last four. Average rank is 240, which is under 2.4% of non-embedding weights and FLOPs. Training used 10,000 C4 samples for 2 epochs, 4 hours on an A100 per predictor. Predictors cost 2.75% of inference time on M1 Max CPU and 4.8% on RTX GPU. They give about 5% false negatives and 7% false positives.
  quote: "These predictors achieve an average of 5% false negatives and 7% false positives in the OPT 6.7B model."
  where: Sec 3.1, App B, C.1
- Predictors cost almost no accuracy on zero-shot tasks.
  number: OPT 6.7B Arc Easy 66.1 -> 66.2, Arc Challenge 30.6 -> 30.6, HellaSwag 50.3 -> 49.8.
  quote: "Arc Easy 66.1 66.2"
  where: Table 1
- Predictors over-predict to avoid false negatives. Predicted-active neurons are 3x actual in OPT and Persimmon, and roughly 2x in Phi-2.
  quote: "the number of active neurons predicted by the predictor is 3x the amount of actual sparsity observed in the case of dense inference"
  where: App B.1
- Other models.
  - Falcon 7B: DRAM use is 52.93% of the model, 33% of the FFN with window 4 and 3.1% of FFN neurons per token. I/O is 161 ms, memory management 90 ms, 250 ms total versus a 2196 ms baseline.
  - Phi-2: gets 2.35x speedup at 65% DRAM.
  - Llama 2 7B: window 2. About 3x speedup over naive. Table 3 gives 3095 -> 994 ms.
  - Persimmon 8B: sigmoid threshold 0.7, FFN memory capped at 25%.
  quote (Falcon): "making our method approximately 9 to 10 times faster."
  quote (Llama 2): "LLM in flash gets 3x speed up over naive baseline (Table 3)."
  where: App C.2-C.5
- MMLU after predictors.
  number: Llama 2 41.8, sparsified 38.96, with predictors 38.63. Phi-2 MMLU drops from 57 to 54.3 after relufication with distillation, then to 52 with predictors.
  quote: "we got MMLU of 41.8 for Llama 2, 38.96 for sparsified model by (Song et al., 2024) and 38.63 after training our predictors."
  where: App C.5, C.4, Fig 10
  note: Table 4 shows Falcon relufied loses accuracy (HellaSwag 57.77 -> 54.17) before predictors, and more with small predictors (50.74).
- Speculative decoding on OPT 6.7B GPU with lambda=4 gives 1.4x, close to the original 1.58x.
  quote: "We used λ = 4and were able to improve the speed of decoding by 1.4x as shown in table 5, this is close to the original 1.58x speedup of speculative decoding."
  where: Sec 5.2
- Memory-latency tradeoff: latency falls as the share of the model kept in DRAM rises (Figure 7, OPT 6.7B on GPU, 35-80% of model in DRAM).
  where: Sec 4.3
- Longer generation does not degrade it. Tested to 1000 tokens, OPT 6.7B on GPU. No SSD thermal throttling, average flash latency does not rise, and nucleus sampling does not hurt.
  where: Sec 5.1
- Negative result: co-activation bundling. The closest friend of each neuron co-activates at least 95% of the time, but bundling it caused repeated loading of highly active neurons.
  quote: "This result suggests that very active neurons are the closest friends of many others."
  where: Sec 3.2, App D
- Memory management. Preallocate per layer Req_i x 2*d_model, swap deleted rows with the last rows, and append new rows. A naive realloc would rewrite about 25% of the FFN.
  where: Sec 3.3, Fig 6
- Small devices (projection only, not measured): a 7B model at 4-bit would need under 2 GB DRAM versus a 3.5 GB baseline. Quantization does not change sparsity (Table 6 average active 3.30% vs 3.27%).
  quote: "rather than the baseline's 3.5GB of required DRAM, our model would necessitate less than 2GB of memory for operation"
  where: App F

LIMITS
- Single-batch inference only. Prompt processing and multi-batch are not studied, and speculative decoding is only preliminary.
- It needs ReLU-type sparsity. OPT is naturally sparse. Falcon, Phi-2 and Llama 2 had to be relufied or FATReLU-finetuned, with some accuracy cost, and it is "constructed on the foundation of sparsified networks". Persimmon already uses squared ReLU.
- Only about half of the model in DRAM was tested. Other ratios are future work.
- Energy: lower power but longer duration, so total energy is higher than dense. Quote: "the sparse model having a higher total energy consumption". No systematic power or thermal study.
- Latency numbers use "best theoretical" I/O for baselines. NVMe throughput was deliberately pessimised (F_NOCACHE, DirectIO, purge), so real figures could be better.
- Test hardware: Apple M1 Max, M2 Ultra, RTX 4090. The 4-bit smartphone case is not implemented, and would need 4-bit kernels. A custom MLX Metal kernel was used because PyTorch MPS has performance cliffs with dynamic shapes.
- Metal M1/M2 speedups are only stated in the intro (7x). The 20x GPU figure is from Naive 2218 ms vs All 84 ms.

BUILDS ON: Dejavu (Liu et al., 2023b) for the low-rank activation predictor. FlexGen (Sheng et al., 2023) for offloading to DRAM and flash. Mirzadeh et al. (2023) for relufication. Song et al. (2024) for FATReLU and sparse Llama 2. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2022). Also HuggingFace Transformers (Wolf et al., 2019), PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019), and the MLX Metal kernels (Hannun et al., 2023). Models: OPT (Zhang et al., 2022b), Falcon, Persimmon, Phi-2, Llama 2. Evaluation: InstructEval (Chia et al., 2023) for MMLU.

CODE: none. The Sec 3.3 data structure fields are pointers, matrix, bias, num_used, last_k_active. Inference uses matrix[:num_rows,:d_model] as up-projection and matrix[:num_rows,d_model:].transpose() as down-projection.

FIGURES (captions read from text, images not viewed)
- Fig 1, p1: stacked bars of per-token latency (compute, load from flash, memory management) for naive vs ours. Half memory. Shows the headline gain at a glance.
- Fig 2, p2: (a) bandwidth/capacity of DRAM vs flash, (b) random-read throughput vs chunk size (4-64 KB) and threads. The case for bundling and parallel reads.
- Fig 3, p4: low-rank predictor structure and false positives/negatives near zero.
- Fig 4, p5: aggregated neuron usage vs window size k, and the sliding-window diagram.
- Fig 5, p6: up-projection column and down-projection row bundled into one read.
- Fig 6, p6: delete/insert memory management.
- Fig 7, p9: latency vs % of model in DRAM (OPT-6.7B, GPU).
- Fig 8, p9: flash latency up to 1000 tokens.
- Fig 9-12, appendix: predicted vs actual sparsity per layer, MMLU vs threshold, perplexity, co-activation.

PROBLEMS
- The Table 2 extraction merges the tick columns. Row 4's configuration is ambiguous, and the "Hybrid / Predictor" header labelling is unclear. The 164 ms row is not tied to a clearly named technique in the extraction. Verify against the PDF before citing individual rows.
- In the Llama 2 appendix, "Gate projects take 13 of FFN layer and 59 of each transformer block" is garbled (fractions 1/3 and 5/9 likely).
- The text has a leftover "«cite nucleus»".
- Figure 1 axis values (100, 450, 700, 1000, 2250, 3100) extracted without clear association. The Llama 2 7B CPU, OPT 6.7B CPU and OPT 6.7B GPU panels show 3100 vs 700 etc., so use Table 3 instead.
- The Persimmon text says 310 ms / 155 ms "as seen in Figure 1" while Table 3 gives total 1041 and Table 5 gives 1090 (310.52 I/O, 155.80 mem). The two tables disagree slightly on Persimmon.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- The venue (ACL 2024) is not stated in the text. Do not cite it as a venue from this source.
